extracted.intended_audience: policymakers, IP scholars, patent practitioners, and biotechnology industry stakeholders
extracted.subtask_description: Analyze and apply U.S. patent subject-matter eligibility principles (35 U.S.C. §101) to biotechnology inventions, with attention to Chakrabarty, Mayo, and Myriad and their policy implications for the biotech industry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 101 statutory categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 101: 'Whoever invents or discovers any new and useful process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter, or any new and useful improvement thereof, may obtain a patent therefor, subject to the conditions and requirements of this title.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the four statutory categories (process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter) as the starting point for determining patentable subject matter. The Supreme Court in Chakrabarty framed the analysis in terms of these categories and quoted the Senate Report's broad formulation ('anything under the sun that is made by man'). Apply these categories before layering later doctrinal limitations from subsequent decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manmade versus naturally occurring distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court distinguished manmade inventions from naturally occurring phenomena; manmade compositions (e.g., genetically modified organisms) can fall within §101 while naturally occurring articles do not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the claimed invention involves human intervention that transforms a natural product into something 'made by man.' Chakrabarty treated the fact that microorganisms are alive as 'a distinction without legal significance' for patent law when they are manmade. Use this distinction to separate patent-eligible claims from naturally occurring matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent eligibility of genetically modified organisms / microorganisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Chakrabarty held that a genetically engineered bacterium constituted patentable subject matter as a 'composition of matter' or 'manufacture.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For claims that involve living organisms, analyze whether the organism is a product of human ingenuity (e.g., genetically altered bacteria, engineered seeds). Chakrabarty supports treating such manmade organisms as eligible; cite Chakrabarty when arguing eligibility for modified biological entities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Isolation/purification as a historic eligibility touchstone
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically, isolating or purifying a component from its natural environment (removing it from its natural milieu) was treated as sufficient to render it patent eligible (Judge Rader's description of his prior practice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing older doctrines or pre‑Myriad cases, consider whether isolation or purification transformed the natural product such that it was sufficiently 'made by man.' Be aware that later Supreme Court decisions (e.g., Myriad) have undercut the sufficiency of mere isolation/purification, so treat this as a historically important but potentially insufficient factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Something more" / 'inventive concept' requirement (post-Mayo/Myriad)
rubrics_metrics.description: Post‑Chakrabarty Supreme Court jurisprudence (Mayo, Myriad) requires more than conventional, routine, or well-known activity — courts look for an 'inventive concept' or 'something more' beyond mere isolation/purification or natural correlations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the claim recites additional inventive features beyond the natural law, natural phenomenon, or routine isolation steps. If the claim merely applies conventional techniques to a natural relationship or to isolated natural products, it risks being held ineligible. The 'something more' inquiry is subjective and fact‑specific; gather evidence showing nonconventionality, inventive steps, or technical improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ineligibility of naturally occurring biological relationships and isolated DNA sequences (Mayo/Myriad holdings)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court in Mayo and Myriad found that naturally occurring biological relationships and isolated DNA sequences are not patent eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When claims recite naturally occurring correlations, laws of nature, or mere isolated native DNA sequences, treat them as vulnerable under Mayo/Myriad. Distinguish claims that add inventive applications or materially different structures from those that simply claim the natural phenomenon or its unaltered sequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on legislative history ('anything under the sun made by man')
rubrics_metrics.description: Chakrabarty relied on legislative history (Senate Report) phrased as 'anything under the sun that is made by man' to interpret §101 expansively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use legislative history to support broad readings of §101 where appropriate; note, however, that later Supreme Court doctrine has introduced judicially created limitations that complicate a purely history-based approach. Cite the Senate Report and Chakrabarty where arguing for expansive eligibility consistent with congressional intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy criterion: patent protection as an incentive for biotechnology innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper treats IP protection—particularly the ability to patent manmade biological inventions—as a key incentive that spurred commercial biotechnology (e.g., genetically modified seeds, PCR, monoclonal antibodies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating policy proposals or legal reforms, weigh how changes to eligibility doctrine will affect incentives for R&D, commercialization, and investment (venture capital flows). Use case studies (Monsanto Roundup Ready, PCR commercialization, Avastin) as illustrative evidence of patent incentives promoting industry growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory and legislative mechanisms that shape biotech commercialization
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutory and policy changes such as the Stevenson‑Wydler Technology Innovation Act and the Bayh‑Dole Act, together with patent eligibility (Chakrabarty), were catalysts for biotech industry growth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In policy analysis, consider the interaction between patent eligibility and other statutory frameworks (tech transfer, federal funding rules). Evaluate whether changes to patent doctrine should be accompanied by legislative or regulatory adjustments (e.g., clarifying §101) to produce predictable incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cluster-growth criteria for biotechnology industries
rubrics_metrics.description: Five synthesized factors for rapid biotech cluster growth: strong science and industry base, funding availability, local entrepreneurial mindset, social networks, and social capital (trust among civic organizations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these five factors when assessing regional or national capacity to develop biotech industries. Policy interventions can be targeted to strengthen one or more factors (e.g., increase funding availability, foster university–industry linkages) to complement patent-policy choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: International/regional constraints (public morality and procedural delay)
rubrics_metrics.description: Other jurisdictions (e.g., under the European Patent Convention) apply public-morality exceptions and other protections that can delay, complicate, or limit patenting in biotech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comparing policy regimes, account for international differences such as public‑morality clauses that can affect the pace and cost of obtaining protection and the geographic location of biotech investment. Use this to argue for or against harmonization or protective exceptions.
